promptText: Why does Spring AI discourage business logic from directly importing a provider-specific class like `OpenAiChatModel`?
options: Because OpenAiChatModel is deprecated and will be removed in a future release
Because it couples business logic to one vendor's SDK, so swapping providers requires rewriting every place that imported the concrete class instead of a single configuration change
Because provider-specific classes cannot be unit tested under any circumstances
Because Spring Boot's classpath scanner ignores provider-specific beans by default
explanation: Depending on ChatModel/ChatClient instead of a concrete provider class means the underlying provider can change via configuration or bean wiring alone, without touching business logic.

promptText: What is the practical difference between `ChatModel` and `ChatClient` in Spring AI?
options: ChatModel and ChatClient are interchangeable aliases for the same interface
ChatModel is the low-level, vendor-neutral interface concrete providers implement; ChatClient is the higher-level fluent API built on top of a ChatModel that application code typically depends on
ChatClient only works with OpenAI, while ChatModel works with all providers
ChatModel is used only for streaming responses, and ChatClient only for non-streaming calls
explanation: ChatModel is the vendor-neutral contract each provider's starter implements; ChatClient wraps a ChatModel with a fluent builder-style API for constructing prompts, attaching advisors, and consuming responses.

promptText: If two `ChatClient` beans are defined and a service injects `ChatClient` by type with no qualifier, what happens at startup?
options: Spring picks the first bean defined alphabetically by bean name
Spring throws a NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException because injection by type alone is ambiguous
Spring silently creates a third, merged ChatClient combining both configurations
The application starts successfully and picks a bean at random per request
explanation: Ambiguous type-based injection with multiple candidate beans fails the application context at startup; disambiguation requires @Qualifier, matching constructor parameter names to bean names, or marking one bean @Primary.

promptText: Which historical Java/Spring precedent is used in the chapter as the direct analogy for why Spring AI models 'a language model' as an interface (ChatModel) rather than a concrete client?
options: The Singleton pattern used for Spring's ApplicationContext
JDBC's DataSource abstraction over vendor-specific database drivers
The Servlet API's HttpServletRequest interface
Java's Comparable interface for sorting collections
explanation: Just as DataSource abstracts over JDBC drivers so application code isn't welded to one database vendor, ChatModel abstracts over LLM providers so business logic isn't welded to one vendor's SDK.

promptText: According to the chapter, what should a routing decision NOT be based on when handling data with strict residency or compliance requirements?
options: The estimated cost of the request
Latency and cost alone, ignoring data sensitivity as a routing input
The user's configured language preference
The time of day the request was made
explanation: The chapter warns that a router built purely for latency/cost reasons can accidentally send sensitive data to an inappropriate model; data sensitivity must be a structurally enforced routing input, not an afterthought.

promptText: What commonly makes a self-hosted model via Ollama a good fit for a fallback tier in a multi-model setup?
options: It has strictly higher reasoning capability than any hosted frontier model
It has zero dependency on any external network call, giving it an independent failure domain from hosted providers
It automatically synchronizes its weights with the primary provider's latest model
It requires no infrastructure provisioning at all
explanation: A locally-hosted model has no shared infrastructure with a hosted cloud provider, so it keeps working during that provider's outage — making it a genuinely independent fallback rather than a false sense of safety.

promptText: A team configures a fallback ChatClient hosted by the same provider as the primary, just on a different endpoint. Why does the chapter call this a false sense of safety?
options: Because Spring AI does not support having two ChatClient beans from the same provider
Because a fallback sharing the same underlying provider is not an independent failure domain — it often fails simultaneously during that provider's own incidents
Because same-provider fallbacks always cost more than switching providers entirely
Because the second endpoint requires a completely separate SDK dependency
explanation: The reliability math (P(served) = 1 − (1−p)(1−q)) only holds under an independence assumption; a same-provider fallback is correlated with the primary's own outages, so it doesn't deliver the redundancy the formula implies.

promptText: How would you correctly wire two differently-tiered ChatClient beans and ensure a specific service uses the strong tier, without hardcoding a provider class into the service?
options: Inject AnthropicChatModel directly into the service constructor
Define two named ChatClient beans built from different ChatModels in a @Configuration class, then inject the desired one into the service via @Qualifier matched to the bean name
Use a static factory method inside the service to instantiate a new ChatClient per call
Set spring.ai.default-model=strong in application.yml and let Spring auto-select the qualifier
explanation: This is the idiomatic Spring AI pattern: named ChatClient beans wired via @Configuration, disambiguated at injection points with @Qualifier, so the service depends only on ChatClient and the qualifier name — never a provider-specific type.

promptText: Why does the chapter warn that setting the same numeric `temperature` value across two different providers does not produce comparably 'creative' output?
options: Because temperature is measured in different units (Celsius-like scale vs. percentage) per provider
Because temperature controls sampling randomness relative to each model's own output distribution, and different models have different underlying distributions
Because only OpenAI's API actually implements the temperature parameter
Because temperature only affects the first token generated, not subsequent tokens
explanation: The same numeric temperature can feel noticeably more or less random depending on the provider's own distribution shape, so temperature tuning generally needs re-validation per model rather than being copied verbatim.

promptText: What is the key architectural difference in how Azure OpenAI is addressed compared to OpenAI directly, and why does it matter for a provider-agnostic abstraction?
options: Azure OpenAI has no API key requirement at all, unlike OpenAI

Azure OpenAI is addressed via a per-tenant endpoint URL and an arbitrary 'deployment name' rather than a well-known public model string, so routing logic must treat the model identifier as an opaque, provider-scoped value
Azure OpenAI only supports streaming responses, never synchronous calls
Azure OpenAI requires a completely different message role vocabulary than OpenAI
explanation: Because the model identifier under Azure OpenAI is a team-chosen deployment name rather than a recognizable public model string, routing/config logic that pattern-matches on 'the model identifier is a well-known string' breaks against Azure.

promptText: A team caches LLM responses keyed only on the prompt text to save cost. What correctness bug does this introduce in a multi-model system?
options: No bug — prompt text alone is always sufficient for a correct cache key
It can silently serve a response generated by model A to a request actually routed to model B, since the cache key doesn't distinguish which model produced it
It causes a cache-stampede where every request bypasses the cache entirely
It doubles the token cost of every cached request
explanation: The cache key must include the model/provider identifier (and relevant options like temperature) alongside the prompt, or a cache hit can serve output from the wrong model for the request actually made — a silent correctness bug, not a crash.

promptText: Why should provider-specific option types like `OpenAiChatOptions` be kept out of shared, generic business logic according to the chapter's best practices?
options: Because provider-specific option classes are marked @Deprecated in Spring AI
Because constructing them deep inside a generic service defeats the abstraction's purpose the moment that service needs to support a second provider
Because they cannot be serialized to JSON for logging
Because they trigger a mandatory schema validation step that slows down every request
explanation: The whole point of the ChatOptions abstraction is that shared business logic stays provider-neutral; reaching for a provider-specific options type inside generic logic reintroduces the coupling the abstraction was built to avoid.

promptText: A staff engineer wants to route 'easy' traffic to a cheap model tier while reserving a strong tier for hard requests. What does the chapter say is the operationally correct way to define 'meets the quality bar' for the cheap tier, given that you cannot evaluate a specific response's quality before it exists?
options: Have the router call an LLM-as-judge on every live request before deciding whether to accept the cheap model's answer

Establish the bar offline per task category, run both models against a labeled evaluation set, and only route live traffic to the cheap tier if its measured pass rate clears an agreed threshold with margin — then re-run periodically or on model version changes
Assume the cheap model is adequate as long as its price is at least 5x lower than the strong model's
Let end users vote per response on which tier should have handled their request going forward
explanation: Since you can't judge a specific response's quality before generating it, the quality bar has to be established offline against representative data; the router then just looks up an approved category rather than judging quality live, and the offline evaluation must be re-run when model versions change.

promptText: Comparing Retry and CircuitBreaker when calling an LLM provider: why does the chapter recommend using both together rather than either alone?
options: Retry and CircuitBreaker perform the exact same function, so combining them is only for redundancy in configuration

Retry handles transient, likely-to-succeed-again failures by re-issuing calls; CircuitBreaker trips open after a sustained failure rate to stop hammering a struggling provider — retry alone can amplify an outage, while circuit-breaker alone gives up on genuine transient blips too eagerly
CircuitBreaker is only relevant for embedding models, while Retry is only relevant for chat models
Using both simultaneously is explicitly discouraged because they conflict at the thread-pool level
explanation: The two mechanisms solve different failure shapes: Retry addresses momentary blips, CircuitBreaker addresses sustained outages by failing fast; using only one leaves a gap the other closes.

promptText: Why does the chapter argue that a broken dynamic router is a more dangerous failure mode than a broken static assignment, and when does it say dynamic routing is actually justified?
options: A dynamic router is never justified in production and should always be avoided in favor of static assignment

Because a bug in the classifier can silently misroute traffic to the wrong tier with no obvious error, adding its own latency/cost/debugging burden; it's justified only when task difficulty genuinely and measurably varies unpredictably within a single feature, demonstrated with data rather than assumed
Because dynamic routers cannot be unit tested under any circumstances, unlike static wiring
Because dynamic routing always costs more in absolute dollar terms than static assignment, regardless of traffic mix
explanation: The risk is an invisible, unmonitored point of failure — a misrouting bug produces no obvious error. The chapter's guidance is to reach for dynamic routing only when static assignment demonstrably cannot express the requirement, evidenced by data.
